title: What is the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy — a forward proxy sits in front of clients and hides them from the server (egress filtering, corporate/VPN, caching outbound requests), while a reverse proxy sits in front of servers and hides them from clients (TLS termination, load balancing, caching, routing) — and which one is Nginx/an API gateway acting as?
shortTitle: What is the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy, and which one is Nginx or an API gateway acting as?

s1_definition.profdef: A forward proxy sits in front of clients and acts on their behalf toward the wider internet: clients send their outbound requests to the forward proxy, which forwards them to destination servers, so the destination sees the proxy's IP rather than the client's. It is used for egress filtering, corporate or VPN access control, anonymity, and caching outbound requests. A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and acts on their behalf toward clients: clients think they are talking to the reverse proxy, which forwards requests to the real backend servers and hides them, providing TLS termination, load balancing, caching, and routing. The direction of "who it hides" is the key difference — a forward proxy hides clients from servers, a reverse proxy hides servers from clients. Nginx and an API gateway, when fronting your backend services, are acting as reverse proxies.
s1_definition.analogy: A forward proxy is like the corporate mailroom at National Bank of India's head office: every employee's outgoing letter goes through the mailroom, which can block letters to disallowed addresses (egress filtering), stamp them all with the head office return address (hiding the individual employee), and keep copies of common replies (caching). The outside world only sees the mailroom, never the individual employee. A reverse proxy is like the bank's public reception desk: customers arriving from outside talk only to reception, which checks their umbrella (TLS termination), decides which department to send them to (routing), sends them to whichever officer is free (load balancing), and keeps the actual back offices hidden. One protects and represents the people going out; the other protects and represents the servers receiving visitors coming in.
s1_definition.oneliner: A forward proxy fronts clients and hides them from servers for egress control and anonymity, a reverse proxy fronts servers and hides them from clients for TLS, routing, and load balancing — and Nginx or an API gateway in front of your services is a reverse proxy.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A forward proxy sits in front of clients and acts on their behalf toward the wider internet: clients send their outbound requests to the forward proxy, which forwards them to destination servers, so the destination sees the proxy's IP rather than the client's. It is used for egress filtering, corporate or VPN access control, anonymity, and caching outbound requests. A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and acts on their behalf toward clients: clients think they are talking to the reverse proxy, which forwards requests to the real backend servers and hides them, providing TLS termination, load balancing, caching, and routing. The direction of "who it hides" is the key difference — a forward proxy hides clients from servers, a reverse proxy hides servers from clients. Nginx and an API gateway, when fronting your backend services, are acting as reverse proxies.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A forward proxy is like the corporate mailroom at National Bank of India's head office: every employee's outgoing letter goes through the mailroom, which can block letters to disallowed addresses (egress filtering), stamp them all with the head office return address (hiding the individual employee), and keep copies of common replies (caching). The outside world only sees the mailroom, never the individual employee. A reverse proxy is like the bank's public reception desk: customers arriving from outside talk only to reception, which checks their umbrella (TLS termination), decides which department to send them to (routing), sends them to whichever officer is free (load balancing), and keeps the actual back offices hidden. **One line to remember:** A forward proxy fronts clients and hides them from servers for egress control and anonymity, a reverse proxy fronts servers and hides them from clients for TLS, routing, and load balancing — and Nginx or an API gateway in front of your services is a reverse proxy.

sections.s2_technical:
The two kinds of proxy are mirror images, and the clearest way to keep them straight is to ask "whose side is the proxy on, and who does it hide?"

A forward proxy is on the client's side. Clients are configured to send their outbound traffic through it, and it relays those requests to arbitrary destination servers on the internet. Because the destination server receives the connection from the proxy, it sees the proxy's IP, not the client's, so the client is hidden. The common uses are egress filtering (a company routes all employee web traffic through a forward proxy that blocks disallowed sites and logs usage), access control and VPN-style gateways (only traffic through the proxy is allowed out), anonymity (the client's identity is masked), and caching of outbound requests (if many employees fetch the same file, the proxy serves a cached copy). A forward proxy typically does not know in advance which servers it will talk to — it can reach any destination the client asks for.

A reverse proxy is on the server's side. It is deployed in front of a known set of backend servers, and external clients connect to it believing it is the server. It forwards each request to the appropriate backend and returns the response, hiding the backends entirely. The common uses are TLS termination (the reverse proxy holds the certificate and decrypts HTTPS so backends can speak plain HTTP), load balancing (spreading requests across backend instances), caching of responses, compression, serving static assets, and routing by path or host. A reverse proxy knows its backends — it is configured with the specific pool of servers it fronts.

The symmetry is: a forward proxy is configured by and serves clients, hiding clients from servers; a reverse proxy is configured by and serves the server operator, hiding servers from clients. The client is aware of a forward proxy (it is configured to use it) but the destination server is not aware of the individual client. With a reverse proxy the client is unaware there are multiple backends behind it, but the server operator deliberately deployed it.

A small conceptual example clarifies. With a forward proxy, an employee's browser is configured with proxy host corporate-proxy:3128, and a request to https://example.com goes browser to corporate-proxy to example.com, and example.com logs the corporate proxy's IP. With a reverse proxy, a customer hits https://bank.example.com, which resolves to the reverse proxy, and the proxy forwards internally to loan-service:8080 or payment-service:8080 based on the path, and the customer never learns those internal hosts exist.

So which is Nginx or an API gateway? It depends on the deployment, but the overwhelmingly common case in a backend system is that Nginx and the API gateway are acting as reverse proxies: they sit in front of your backend services, terminate TLS, route by path, load-balance across instances, and hide the services from clients. Nginx can be configured as a forward proxy too, but when you put it at the front of your microservices it is a reverse proxy, and an API gateway is always a specialized reverse proxy because its entire purpose is to front and protect your backend APIs. A senior nuance is that the same physical software (Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy) can serve either role depending on configuration, so the role is defined by position and purpose, not by the product name; the question to ask is always whether it is fronting clients going out (forward) or servers receiving traffic (reverse).
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India has two separate proxy needs, and the team keeps confusing them.

Problem 1 — Controlling what employees reach. The bank must ensure employees' machines can only reach approved external sites and that all outbound traffic is logged for compliance, while hiding individual employee IPs from external sites. This is a forward proxy: it fronts the clients (employees) and hides them from the external servers, doing egress filtering and outbound caching.

Problem 2 — Protecting and routing to internal services. Customers from the internet must reach the loan and payment services, but those services must be hidden, TLS must be terminated in one place, and traffic must be routed by path and spread across instances. This is a reverse proxy: it fronts the servers and hides them from clients, doing TLS termination, routing, and load balancing. Nginx or the API gateway plays this role.

We will model both proxies so the difference is unmistakable. A `ForwardProxy` takes employee requests to external sites, applies egress filtering, masks the client, and caches outbound responses. A `ReverseProxy` takes customer requests, terminates TLS, routes by path to a backend, and hides the backend.

The code will have a `ForwardProxy` with an allowlist and an outbound cache, a `ReverseProxy` with path routing and TLS termination, backend representations, and a demo that runs an employee reaching an allowed and a blocked site through the forward proxy, and a customer reaching the loan and payment services through the reverse proxy.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: employee Rajesh reaches npci.org.in twice then facebook.com through the forward proxy; customers reach /api/loans and /api/payments through the reverse proxy.

Step 1 — Rajesh's outbound request to npci.org.in enters the forward proxy. The proxy checks its allowlist, sees npci.org.in is allowed, and relays it. The destination sees the proxy's IP, not Rajesh's machine — the client is hidden. This is the forward proxy fronting the client.

Step 2 — Rajesh's second request to npci.org.in is served from the forward proxy's outbound cache, so it never leaves the building — outbound caching in action.

Step 3 — Priya's request to facebook.com hits the forward proxy, which finds it is not on the allowlist and blocks it, logging the attempt for compliance — egress filtering.

Step 4 — Now a customer from the internet sends /api/loans to the reverse proxy. The reverse proxy terminates TLS (it holds the certificate), looks up the route for /api/loans, and forwards to loan-service:8080. The customer never learns that internal host exists — the server is hidden. This is the reverse proxy fronting the servers.

Step 5 — Another customer sends /api/payments; the reverse proxy routes it to payment-service:8080. The same component hides multiple backends behind one public address, which is exactly what Nginx or an API gateway does in front of your services.

Step 6 — The contrast is clear in the logs: the forward proxy decisions are about which client may reach which external destination and hiding the client, while the reverse proxy decisions are about which internal backend serves a path and hiding the backend.

```
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] === FORWARD PROXY (fronts clients, hides them from servers) ===
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] FORWARD relayed EMP-Rajesh → npci.org.in (dest sees proxy IP, employee hidden)
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] FORWARD served CACHED copy of npci.org.in to EMP-Rajesh
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [WARNING] FORWARD blocked EMP-Priya → facebook.com (not on allowlist)
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] === REVERSE PROXY (fronts servers, hides them from clients) ===
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] REVERSE terminated TLS for customer-SAV2001
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] REVERSE routed /api/loans → loan-service:8080 (client never sees backend host)
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] BACKEND loan-service:8080 served /api/loans
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] REVERSE terminated TLS for customer-CUR3001
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] REVERSE routed /api/payments → payment-service:8080 (client never sees backend host)
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] BACKEND payment-service:8080 served /api/payments
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A forward proxy and a reverse proxy are mirror images, and the cleanest way to tell them apart is to ask whose side the proxy is on and who it hides. A forward proxy is on the client's side: clients are configured to send their outbound traffic through it, it relays those requests to destination servers, and because the destination receives the connection from the proxy it sees the proxy's IP rather than the client's, so the client is hidden. Forward proxies are used for egress filtering, corporate or VPN access control, anonymity, and caching of outbound requests.

A reverse proxy is on the server's side: it sits in front of a known set of backend servers, external clients connect to it believing it is the server, and it forwards each request to the right backend while hiding the backends entirely. Reverse proxies handle TLS termination where the proxy holds the certificate so backends speak plain HTTP, load balancing across instances, caching, compression, and routing by path or host.

The symmetry I always state is that a forward proxy hides clients from servers and a reverse proxy hides servers from clients. In my bank example the forward proxy fronted employees, enforced an allowlist so only approved external sites were reachable, logged egress for compliance, and masked employee IPs, while the reverse proxy fronted the internal services, terminated TLS in one place, routed by path to the loan and payment services, and kept those internal hosts invisible to customers.

As for which one Nginx or an API gateway is, the answer in a backend system is almost always a reverse proxy: when they sit in front of your services terminating TLS, routing, and load balancing, they are reverse proxies, and an API gateway is always a specialized reverse proxy because its whole purpose is to front and protect your backend APIs. The nuance I add is that the same software such as Nginx, HAProxy, or Envoy can play either role depending on configuration, so the role is defined by position and purpose, not by the product name.

The one-line summary I give is: a forward proxy fronts clients and hides them from servers for egress control and anonymity, a reverse proxy fronts servers and hides them from clients for TLS, routing, and load balancing, and Nginx or an API gateway placed in front of your services is acting as a reverse proxy.
